questions.learningObjective: compose two translations into a single translation by adding vectors

forgets the first slide and uses only the second

questions.subject: GEOMETRY

questions.learningObjective: explain why a reflection reverses orientation even though it preserves lengths
questions.stem: A student claims that reflecting a triangle across a line cannot change its orientation, because a reflection preserves every side length and so must simply slide the triangle to a new spot. What is the error in that reasoning?

options.text: Preserved lengths do not force a slide; the mirror flips the vertex order
Reflection is not rigid, so a mirror step must change the side lengths
options.misconception: believes only rotations count as rigid motions

options.text: A mirror step reverses only the side lengths and not the vertex order
options.misconception: believes a reflection scrambles lengths but keeps order

options.text: A mirror step is really a quarter turn dressed up as a reflection
options.misconception: believes every reflection hides an extra quarter turn

questions.explanation: A reflection is rigid, so it does preserve all three side lengths, but rigid motions split into two families: those that keep the winding order of the vertices, such as translations and rotations, and those that reverse it, such as a single reflection. Take the corners (0, 0), (4, 0), and (0, 3), which run counterclockwise; mirrored over the y-axis they become (0, 0), (-4, 0), and (0, 3), which run clockwise with every length unchanged. So the flaw is the step from preserved lengths to preserved order: the reasoning is tempting because length preservation really is the mark of every rigid motion, but orientation is a separate property, which is why B, C, and D each misdescribe it.
questions.hint: Track the order of the vertices before and after the mirror step.

questions.learningObjective: apply the fact that a rotation preserves the distance from its center
questions.stem: A point P sits 6 units from the center C of a Ferris wheel. The wheel turns, carrying P around C by some rotation, and P arrives at a new point P'. How far is P' from C?

options.text: 6 units
0 units
options.misconception: believes every rotation drives the point onto the center

options.text: 12 units
options.misconception: doubles the radius as if the wheel grew during the turn

options.text: 3 units
options.misconception: halves the radius as if the turn shrank the wheel

questions.explanation: A rotation is a rigid motion about its center, so every point keeps the radius it started with: P stays 6 units from C, and its whole path is the circle of radius 6 around that center. 0 units would mean the point landed on the center, which no rotation does, 12 units doubles the radius as though the wheel grew, and 3 units halves it as though the turn deflated the wheel. Dividing or multiplying the radius is the mistake of applying a dilation where a rotation belongs, since only a dilation rescales distances from its center.
questions.hint: A rotation sweeps points around a circle whose radius never changes.

questions.learningObjective: apply a dilation whose center is not the origin
questions.stem: A model airplane is drawn on a grid as a horizontal segment with endpoints (3, 1) and (7, 1), so it is 4 units long and level. A droid sits at the point (3, 1) and serves as the center of a dilation with scale factor 3, and the segment is enlarged about that center, pushing the endpoint at (7, 1) farther out to the right. triples the offset but flips the vertical direction
collapses the segment onto the center, as a factor of 0 does

Multiplying the raw coordinates instead gives (21, 3), which quietly uses the origin as the center, and (3, 1) would be a factor of 0, the most total collapse there is.
questions.hint: Measure from the center, scale the offset, then add the center back.

questions.learningObjective: scale every side length by the absolute value of a negative scale factor
questions.stem: A triangular garden has side lengths 5 yards, 6 yards, and 7 yards, so its perimeter is 18 yards. A map of the garden is produced by a dilation with scale factor -2 about some center. What is the perimeter, in yards, of the garden on that map?

18 yards

options.misconception: scales the perimeter by the square of the factor, as area scales

options.text: -36 yards
options.misconception: keeps the negative sign on a measured perimeter

Leaving the perimeter at 18 ignores the dilation, 72 squares the factor, which is the rule for areas rather than lengths, and -36 keeps a sign no measurement can carry.

questions.learningObjective: scale the area of a figure by the square of the scale factor
questions.stem: A round pizza has radius 5 inches. A second pizza is a dilation of the first with scale factor 3, taken about the center of the pizza. What is the area, in terms of pi, of the second pizza in square inches?

questions.stem: A painted motif on one wall is reflected into the opposite wall, whose grid line is x = 0, and the copy is then slid 3 units upward along that wall. The motif contains a point originally at (2, -1). Which claim must be true about the final copy?

It enlarges every distance in the motif by the length of the slide

questions.learningObjective: compose two reflections over parallel lines into one translation
questions.stem: A point P sits at (0, 0) on a grid. First P is reflected over the horizontal line y = 1, and then the resulting point is reflected over the parallel line y = 4. In which direction, and by how many units, has the final point moved from P?

options.text: 6 units straight up
3 units straight up
options.misconception: measures the gap between the lines instead of twice the gap

options.text: 2 units straight up
options.misconception: stops after the first reflection's move of two units

options.text: 6 units straight down
options.misconception: sends the point away from the second mirror line

questions.explanation: Two reflections over parallel lines combine into a single translation of twice the distance from the first line to the second. The lines y = 1 and y = 4 are 3 units apart, and the rule gives a slide of 2 * 3 = 6 units. Step by step, (0, 0) reflects over y = 1 to (0, 2), and (0, 2) reflects over y = 4 to (0, 6), which is 6 units above the starting point, in the direction of the second mirror. Using the 3-unit gap leaves the point short, and 2 units is only the first reflection's own move.
questions.hint: Reflect the point in both lines and measure the total move it makes.

questions.learningObjective: identify a half turn as the composite of reflections over two perpendicular lines
questions.stem: A student reflects a point across the x-axis and then across the y-axis, and claims the two steps together must be a translation, because two moves in a row always add up to one slide. What is the error in that claim?

options.text: The two steps give a half turn about the origin, not a translation
The two steps give a translation of two units along each axis at once
options.misconception: believes the two steps add into a single slide of double length

options.text: The two steps give a reflection across the line where the axes cross
options.misconception: believes the composite is a mirror across the diagonal

options.text: The two steps give a dilation of scale factor negative one unit
options.misconception: believes negating both coordinates is a shrink-and-flip dilation

questions.explanation: Translations add because they share a direction and length, but a reflection is not a translation, so the shortcut does not apply here. Reflecting (x, y) over the x-axis gives (x, -y), and reflecting that over the y-axis gives (-x, -y), the rule for a 180-degree turn about the origin. A translation would carry (3, 0) and (0, 2) in one common direction by one common length, and these two images head in opposite directions instead, so no single slide explains both. Negating both coordinates is also what a dilation of factor -1 does, but describing the motion honestly means naming the two reflections that produced it.
questions.hint: Work out the actual image of one off-axis point under both steps.

questions.learningObjective: explain why a dilation of factor -1 and a half turn describe one map
questions.stem: A dilation about the origin with scale factor -1 sends a point (a, b) to (-a, -b), and a 180-degree rotation about the origin also sends (a, b) to (-a, -b). Which statement correctly explains why the two names describe one and the same map?

options.text: Both send every point across the origin, so the images coincide
Both flip only one coordinate, so the images coincide as well
options.misconception: believes each map negates just one of the two coordinates

options.text: Both are dilations, so the images must match for any factor
options.misconception: believes the name alone forces two maps to agree

options.text: Both are rigid motions, so the images must be the same point
options.misconception: believes rigidity makes every rigid motion identical

questions.explanation: Two transformations coincide when they send every point to the same image, and both formulas produce (-a, -b) for every input, so the maps are identical and each point lands directly across the origin from itself, twice its distance out. Flipping only one coordinate, as (a, -b) or (-a, b) would, describes a mirror, and neither map flips just one. A shared name proves nothing, since a translation and a dilation of factor 1 both slide points and yet move them differently, and rigidity proves nothing either, since a quarter turn is rigid and lands every point somewhere else.
questions.hint: Compare the image of one concrete point such as (2, 3) under each map.

questions.learningObjective: find the translation vector that carries a given point onto the origin
questions.stem: A bug sits at the point (7, -4) on a coordinate grid. One translation is chosen so that the bug lands exactly on the origin, and that translation's vector is written as (h, k). What is the vector (h, k)?

options.misconception: signs the vertical part of the vector the wrong way
reverses the whole vector instead of moving to the origin
leaves the vector equal to the starting point's coordinates

questions.explanation: The vector must satisfy (7 + h, -4 + k) = (0, 0), which forces h = -7 and k = 4, so the vector is (-7, 4), meaning 7 units left and 4 units up. Reading the signs the other way, (7, 4) would put the bug at (14, 0) and (-7, -4) at (0, -8), both of which land on an axis but not at the origin. (7, -4) is the starting point's own coordinate pair, which is no move at all and would leave the bug exactly where it sits.
questions.hint: Set each coordinate of the image to 0 and solve for the two parts of the vector.

questions.learningObjective: identify a transformation from two point-image pairs and rule out the rivals
questions.stem: In a coordinate plane, P sits at (6, 2) with image P' at (2, 6), and Q sits at (1, 5) with image Q' at (5, 1). One transformation is applied to the whole plane that carries P to P' and Q to Q'. Which transformation is it?

options.text: A reflection across the line y = x
A 180-degree turn about the origin
options.misconception: matches P to P' but not Q to Q'

options.text: A 90-degree counterclockwise turn about the origin
options.misconception: sends P into the second quadrant, not to P'

options.text: A translation of 4 units straight up
options.misconception: raises both points instead of swapping coordinates

questions.explanation: A reflection across y = x swaps coordinates, so P goes to (2, 6) and Q goes to (5, 1), matching both pairs at once, and the midpoint of P and P' is (4, 4) with the joining segment at slope -1, exactly the mirror geometry. A half turn would send P to (-6, -2) and Q to (-1, -5), and a quarter turn counterclockwise would send P to (-2, 6), which sits in the second quadrant rather than at P'. The two pairs are what make the answer certain: the only quarter turn that fits P is centered at (2, 2), and that center sends Q to (-1, 1) instead of (5, 1).
questions.hint: Test each candidate on P first, then keep only the one that also fits Q.

questions.learningObjective: find the net effect of composing a reflection with a rotation
questions.stem: One transformation is applied to the whole plane: first a reflection across the line y = x, then a 90-degree counterclockwise rotation about the origin. What is the net effect of sending a point through both steps in that order?

options.text: A reflection across the y-axis, sending (x, y) to (-x, y)
A reflection across the x-axis, sending (x, y) to (x, -y)
options.misconception: reverses the order of the two steps in the working

options.text: A 90-degree counterclockwise turn about the origin
options.misconception: drops the reflection and keeps only the turn

options.text: A 180-degree turn about the origin
options.misconception: adds the two steps' angles as if both were turns

questions.explanation: Apply the steps in order to a general point: the reflection sends (x, y) to (y, x), and the quarter turn then sends (y, x) to (-x, y), which is the rule for a mirror across the y-axis. A sample confirms it, since (4, 7) reflects to (7, 4) and then turns to (-4, 7), exactly where the y-axis mirror puts it. The other three candidates come from mixing up the steps, discarding one of them, or adding a mirror's flip to a turn's angle, and none of them can be right anyway, because a composition containing a single reflection reverses orientation, which no turn ever does.
questions.hint: Run an arbitrary point through both steps and name the map that results.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY

questions.learningObjective: track a point through a three-step composition in the stated order
questions.stem: A mural drawn at the point (4, 1) is first reflected across the vertical wall line x = 0, then the copy is slid 2 units up along that wall, and finally the whole mural is translated 5 units right. A student runs the steps in a different order, translating 5 units right first and mirroring last, and lands at (-9, 3). Which option names the error and the correct landing point?

options.text: Run the steps as given; the point lands at (1, 3)
Run the steps as given; the point lands at (9, 3)
options.misconception: reads the mirror as a slide and keeps the point on its own side

options.text: The steps may run in any order; the point lands at (1, 3)
options.misconception: believes reflections and slides can be freely reordered

options.text: The steps may run in any order; the point lands at (9, 3)
options.misconception: believes order is free and mirrors in the wrong direction

questions.explanation: The order matters, because reflecting over x = 0 negates the horizontal coordinate while translations only add amounts, and those two operations do not commute. Running the steps as given, (4, 1) reflects to (-4, 1), the 2-unit slide gives (-4, 3), and the 5-unit shift gives (1, 3). Running the translation first puts the point at (9, 1) before the mirror, and mirroring that yields (-9, 3), the student's landing, which sits 10 units too far left, the amount of the double negation of the 5-unit shift. (9, 3) reads the mirror's sign backwards, and claiming any order works would make mirrors and slides interchangeable, which they are not.
questions.hint: Apply the three steps one at a time in the order the mural description gives them.
